Learning Objectives
Discuss the appropriate workup for a patient with a newly discovered unknown lesion of the
spine, including pertinent patient history, physical examination, imaging studies, and
laboratory studies.
Review the correct principles for performing a biopsy.
Identify the main primary bone tumors of the spine.
Review the natural history of benign and malignant tumors of the spine.
Explain the value of a multidisciplinary spine tumor group.
Review surgical and nonsurgical treatment options for primary bone tumors of the spine.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview and Epidemiology

Primary bone tumors of the spine are rare. Approximately 50 patients are diagnosed with
metastatic disease of the spine for every one patient diagnosed with a primary tumor of the
spine. Primary bone tumors throughout the body are rare, and tumors within the spine
represent only approximately 5% to 10% of all primary bone tumors,.1,2 Given the rare nature
of these tumors, recognizing them and understanding the appropriate workup and
management are critical. Surgeons should be familiar with the most common of these rare
tumors.
Common malignant primary tumors of the spine
Chordoma
Osteosarcoma
Chondrosarcoma
Ewing sarcoma
Common benign primary tumors of the spine
Hemangioma
Aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC)
Giant cell tumor (GCT)
A new spinal lesion requires appropriate workup and diagnosis, including appropriate imaging
studies, staging studies, and tissue biopsy (Table 1; Figure 1).
Although rare situations may arise in which surgical management is necessary to prevent
catastrophic neurologic compromise, every effort should be made to establish a tissue
diagnosis so an appropriate multidisciplinary overall plan (radiation therapy, chemotherapy,
surgical management) can be created and appropriate margins can be achieved surgically.
The anatomy, biomechanics, and nearby structures must be well understood.
Table 1 Workup for Unknown Spinal Lesions or Tumors
MRI of the entire spine with and without contrast
CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis
CT of the area of interest in the spine
Plain radiographs of the area of interest (upright)
Complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive
protein level

studies must be ordered for patients with a new spinal lesion. This should include plain

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Biomechanics (Sagittal Balance)
Large spine tumor resection should only be undertaken with the proper understanding of
spinal deformity principles, particularly sagittal balance. For example, understanding the
relationship between pelvic incidence and lumbar lordosis is critical (Figure 2).

Figure 2 Illustration shows measurement of pelvic incidence, which is determined based on
the sacral slope and pelvic tilt. (Reproduced from Hu SS, Wood KB: Sagittal imbalance of the
spine, in Truumees E, Prather H, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Spine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 362-369.)
Vasculature
Tumor blood supply
Spinal tumors can be vascular, and preoperative embolization often is preferred.
Embolization of vessels, if possible, may substantially decrease the risk of bleeding
intraoperatively. Ideally, embolization should be performed 24 to 72 hours preoperatively,
and spine surgeons should examine patients after embolization but preoperatively to assess
for deficits.
Examples of tumors that may benefit from embolization are ABCs and atypical hemangiomas
requiring resection.
Spinal cord blood supply

Some surgeons advocate clamping a nerve root and its vessel to evaluate for intraoperative
monitoring signal changes before tying and dividing; however, most surgeons do not use this
method because it is not reliable for predicting neurologic deficits and the delay from
clamping to signal change varies widely.
With regard to the vasculature of the spinal cord, as much as three-level bilateral nerve root
sacrifice in spine tumor surgery, even in the lower thoracic spine, often is well tolerated
without neurologic deficits.

Vasculature
Understanding the blood supply to the spinal cord is critical in the surgical management
of spinal tumors because tumor resection may involve resection of a nerve root with its
spinal branch off of the intercostal artery (Figures 3 and 4). Thirty-one paired radicular
arteries arise from spinal branches, all of which are paired with a nerve root. In the
thoracic spine, the spinal branches arise from the intercostal artery.

Nerves
Resection of a primary tumor of the spine may require resection of one or more nerve roots,
either to obtain adequate margins or for reconstruction. Understanding when and where
nerve roots can be resected is critical to surgical planning. In terms of the severity of
consequences of nerve root sacrifice, thoracic nerve roots are associated with the least
consequences, followed by the sacral, cervical, and lumbar nerve roots, in that order (Table 2).

Thoracic Nerve Roots
Most commonly, a thoracic nerve root may need to be ligated to access a tumor or work safely
under the spinal cord. Most thoracic nerve roots can be tied off without any adverse effects.
Considerable effort has been made to determine how many nerve roots can be sacrificed and
whether the deficit that would result from ligating a root, with its potential blood supply to the
spinal cord, can be safely predicted. Because thoracic nerve roots supply mainly skin sensation
in the radicular area around the ribs, they can be sacrificed without substantial deficits.
Although most thoracic nerves contribute a small amount to small trunk muscles, the T11-12
nerves may have a more noticeable effect because of their innervation of abdominal muscles.
T1 should not be sacrificed because it contributes to the brachial plexus and hand function.
Given the possible pre-fixed and post-fixed variations of the plexus, T2 also may play a role in
hand function in some patients.

Ligating thoracic nerve roots below T6 has little to no effect on the sympathetic tone of most
blood vessels. Only if spinal cord injuries are above T6 is autonomic dysfunction of this nature
typically observed. Ligating nerve roots below T6 is unlikely to affect autonomic function.
Sacral Nerve Roots
Although occasionally necessary for en bloc resection, removing sacral nerve roots may result
in substantial morbidity. Typically, this removal is discussed in the setting of sacrectomy for a
sacral tumor, in which part or all of the sacrum is resected en bloc and part or all of the sacral
nerve roots must be ligated.
Sacrificing S1 roots will affect a patient’s motor function and ability to push off when walking.
Sacrificing one of the S2 nerve roots (and below) will leave most patients incontinent.
If both S3 nerve roots and above can be left intact, most patients will maintain relatively
normal bowel, bladder, and sexual function.
Sacrificing S4 and S5 may have effects; however, the effects often are limited to some
perianal numbness and occasional sexual dysfunction.
Unless nerve root sacrifice is necessary to achieve a life-preserving negative margin, the
preference is to preserve the S3 nerve roots if possible.
Cervical Nerve Roots
Cervical nerve roots should be preserved if possible; however, achieving an adequate tumor
margin may require sacrifice of selected levels.
Sacrificing C2 bilaterally can be performed uneventfully.
Resection of C2 is performed routinely in C1-2 fusions and causes little more than some
residual numbness on the posterior scalp.
Sacrificing C3 and C4 unilaterally often can be performed uneventfully.
Bilateral C3-4 ligation may have effects on the diaphragm and should be avoided.
Ligation of nerve roots contributing to the brachial plexus (C5 through T1) should be avoided.
If one root must be removed because of a tumor, careful patient counseling is required. The
C7 nerve root may be the most redundant, and its sacrifice is better tolerated than other nerve
root sacrifice; however, deficits are still be expected.
Lumbar Nerve Roots

In general, lumbar nerve root sacrifice should be avoided because any sacrifice has direct
debilitating effects on the patient. If a root must be sacrificed with resection of a tumor, the
patient must be counseled carefully. Patients who undergo sacrifice of L2 or L3 may require a
locking hinged knee brace to ambulate because they often are unable to lock the knee
straight.
Etiology and Natural History
Many primary tumors arise from various multifactorial causes and/or for reasons not fully
understood.
Because of their proximity to the spinal cord and nerve roots, many seemingly benign lesions
can become symptomatic and warrant resection.
Classification Systems
Numerous methods of classifying tumors have been developed over the years.
Benign tumors versus malignant tumors versus tumor mimickers
Malignant spine tumors
Benign spine tumors
Tumor mimickers (eg, infection, brown tumor, Paget disease, hemangioma, bone island,
sarcoid, tuberculosis)
Location (anterior versus posterior aspect of bone)
Vertebral body (eg, hemangioma, GCT, chondrosarcoma, osteosarcoma)
Posterior elements (eg, osteoid osteoma, ABC, osteoblastoma)
Location (extradural, intradural extramedullary, or intramedullary)
Extradural (eg, primary bone tumors)
Intradural extramedullary (eg, nerve sheath tumors [schwannoma, neurofibroma],
meningioma, myxopapillary ependymoma)
Intradural intramedullary (eg, astrocytoma, ependymoma, hemangioblastoma)
Patient Age
Adult (eg, chordoma, chondrosarcoma, osteosarcoma)
Pediatric (eg, Ewing sarcoma, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, osteochondroma, osteosarcoma)
Staging and Enneking-Appropriate Margins
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:50 PM

The concept of Enneking-appropriate margins grew out of the extremity literature and
currently applies to spine tumors. As applied to limb tumors, the classic terminology referred
to radical, wide, marginal, and intralesional resection margins (Figure 5). Because spine
tumors often do not allow for radical or even wide excision because of the presence of the
neural elements, many tumors are excised with close margins, particularly if the tumor
approaches the dura. The classic Enneking staging system for sarcomas is listed in Table 3.
In referring to spinal tumor margins, the term Enneking-appropriate currently often refers to
the margin that is most favorable for long-term outcomes for patient.
For example, successful resection of chordoma depends on removal of all tumor cells to
prevent recurrence; however, chordoma can recur even after R0 resection. This recurrence is
thought to be partly because of micrometastases lurking outside the tumor margin, up to 2
cm away.
Advances in radiation oncology have improved durable outcomes in chordoma management;
however, complete excision of chordoma is preferred.
The term en bloc, literally translated, means all together or at the same time. In discussing
Enneking-appropriate margins and spinal tumors, the term en bloc typically means not only
resecting the tumor all together but doing so with a negative margin and without violating
the tumor (in contrast to piecemeal resection).
The appropriate margin is determined by the final pathology rather than the surgical
approach.

American Joint Committee on Cancer and Weinstein-Boriani-Biagini Staging Systems
Although the concept of Enneking-appropriate margins is appealing clinically, the American
Joint Committee on Cancer staging system (eighth edition) currently offers a classification for
primary spine tumors. Based on the TNM classification system (tumor size, nodes, metastasis),
a T category describes spine-specific parameters.
The Weinstein-Boriani-Biagini system was introduced in the late 1990s and has been used to
classify primary tumors of the spine and to aid in planning resection.
Evaluation and Diagnosis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:50 PM
AAOS | Primary Bone Tumors of the Spine

13/34

The correct recognition, staging, and diagnosis of a new spinal lesion is of utmost importance.
If a spinal lesion of unknown origin is present, identification of the lesion should follow a fairly
standardized workup.
Patient history and physical examination include the following:
Any other current or prior malignancies or proliferative disorders
Travel/infectious disease history
CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis to assess for other tumors
MRI of the entire spine, with and without contrast, to identify other lesions within the spine
Plain radiographs (upright if possible) of the area of interest in the spine
Dedicated CT reconstruction images of the area of interest (or from CT scans of the chest,
abdomen, and pelvis)
Serum protein electrophoresis, urine protein electrophoresis, and other tests that may be of
value (eg, prostate-specific antigen)
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein level, complete blood count, comprehensive
metabolic panel
Tissue biopsy
Tissue biopsy is the preferred method for identifying a new spinal lesion; however, complete
imaging of the spine (MRI of the entire spine, with and without contrast, and CT of the chest,
abdomen, and pelvis) often should be completed first. If a lesion is identified as metastatic,
tissue may be obtained from a more convenient site than that originally identified. Typically,
all imaging and laboratory studies can be ordered as plans for biopsy are being made.
Consideration of multidisciplinary tumor board
Because of the rapid advancement in spine tumor management in the past 20 years, the
author of this lesson encourages all institutions to use a multidisciplinary tumor board.
Advances in chemotherapy and targeted therapies, radiation oncology, interventional
radiology, and surgery have made mastering of spine tumor management nearly impossible
for one provider. Care can be optimized if a group of experts from each area discuss most or
all cases.
In patients with rapid neurologic deterioration, time for a biopsy may not be available because
results may take 5 to 7 days. Surgeons must ask the patient how much has changed in the past
day or past week. Some patients will report rapid neurologic decline within 24 hours and
should not await a biopsy. Other patients will report decline over 1 week or more; often, these
patients may benefit from steroids while awaiting biopsy results. Typically, steroids are used
only after biopsy is performed because they may interfere with results for lesions such as
lymphoma.

The tissue diagnosis is important to determine before surgical management because it is
critical in achieving an appropriate margin for cure or durable response. In addition, some
lesions do not require surgical management despite their appearance and may be managed
via radiation therapy (lymphoma) or may not require surgical management or radiation
therapy (eg, sarcoid).
Imaging Studies
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Classic malignant lesions appear bright on T2-weighted MRIs, appear dark on T1-weighted
MRIs, and enhance with contrast. This pattern, although classic for malignant lesions, does not
by itself confirm a diagnosis of malignancy.
Classic nontumor MRI patterns
Hemangioma: bright on T1-weighted MRIs, bright on T2-weighted MRIs (confirm with CT
showing trabecula)
Bone island (sclerosis): dark on T1-weighted MRIs, dark on T2-weighted MRIs
Brown tumor: dark on T1-weighted MRIs, variable on T2-weighted MRIs, enhances with
contrast
Paget disease: bright on T1-weighted MRIs, dark on T2-weighted MRIs, enhances with
contrast
Synovial cysts: from facet joint, rim enhances with contrast (because of fluid)
Other MRI patterns
Typically, osteodiscitis/infections begin in the disk space and spread to end plates and bone.
Typically, tumors begin in the bone and often are disk sparing. Atypical infections, such as
tuberculosis, fungal infections, or brucellosis, also may be disk sparing and mimic spinal
tumors on imaging studies.
Radiography
Radiographs should always be included for sagittal alignment and localization, among other
reasons. A preoperative radiograph can immediately identify the whole picture of a patient’s
condition (is the soft-tissue density close to that of the bone?), provide a preview of a localizing
intraoperative radiograph, and demonstrate any hardware or foreign body that may be
present. In addition, if upright images are possible, the surgeon can begin to plan for
reconstruction.

Computed Tomography
Typically, CT of the spine in the area of interest is helpful. CT scans will help delineate
calcification, bone destruction, and so on.
Positron Emission Tomography/Bone Scintigraphy
Positron emission tomography (PET)/bone scintigraphy may be used depending on the tumor
but typically is not a first-line imaging modality and should not be used instead of full spine
MRI because some nontumor lesions appear bright on PET, resolution often is lower than of
full spine MRI, and some tumors appear cold on PET.
Laboratory Studies
Serum protein electrophoresis, urine protein electrophoresis, erythrocyte sedimentation rate,
C-reactive protein level, complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, and other pertinent
laboratory studies as appropriate (eg, prostate-specific antigen)
Diagnosis
A diagnosis requires a tissue biopsy.
Local recurrence
In patients with local recurrence, the physician may be tempted to skip a new tissue biopsy;
however, patients may have two different malignancies, and a local recurrence may be
related to local treatment, such as a radiation-induced sarcoma. In general, skipping the
biopsy is not advised.
Rapid neurologic decline
Rapid neurologic compromise may force the physician to skip the tissue biopsy. In these
patients, surgeons should perform a careful dissection, decompress the neural elements,
obtain a piece of tumor for biopsy, and seal off the tumor before closure. In this manner, the
neural elements can be relieved, and a tissue biopsy can be obtained. After the biopsy
results are obtained, the patient may return for appropriate surgical treatment.
Nondiagnostic biopsy
Occasionally, the biopsy may be nondiagnostic. In this situation, the biopsy can be repeated
or sent to another pathologist for additional review.
Final diagnosis

16/34

Final diagnosis is not made until the final specimen is resected and reviewed by a
pathologist. The patient should be warned that the diagnosis may change before it is
finalized.
Biopsy principles
The biopsy should be performed by an experienced spine tumor physician. Often, this
physician is a musculoskeletal radiologist or interventional radiologist. The needle is
advanced down a tube such that the surrounding tissue is not contaminated. Core biopsies
are used to obtain tissue from spine tumors because they provide better tissue samples and
lower rates of nondiagnostic biopsies than techniques such as fine-needle aspiration biopsy.
Typically, the biopsy is kept midline to allow for surgical removal of the biopsy tract; however,
the utility of removing this tract remains questionable in spine tumor surgery.
No other cavity or compartment should be violated during the biopsy unless necessary. For
example, a biopsy involving the sacrum should never be performed through the rectum, and
a biopsy involving the upper cervical spine should not be performed through the
oropharynx.
Differential Diagnosis
Use of the terms malignant and benign in reference to primary spinal tumors may be
problematic. Some tumors that are histologically benign can be destructive and lead to
paralysis (eg, ABC). Tumors technically classified as low-grade malignancies may have a strong
proclivity for local recurrence and require aggressive en bloc resection with the widest margin
possible (eg, chordoma). In addition, some so-called benign lesions can metastasize to the
lungs, with substantial mortality after metastatic disease to the lungs is diagnosed (eg, GCT of
bone). Malignant and aggressive lesions can be classified together, in contrast to benign and
nonaggressive spinal lesions.
Common benign or nonaggressive tumors of the spine
Hemangioma (Figure 6)
Benign vascular tumor
Common incidental finding (approximately 10% of the population)
Age: seen in individuals of all ages
Location: commonly vertebral body
Imaging studies
Bright on T1-weighted MRIs, bright on T2-weighted MRIs
Atypical lipid-poor variants may appear dark (isointense) on T1-weighted MRIs

Management
Surgical indications remain similar to those for metastatic disease: instability or cord/root
compression. Otherwise, these tumors do not need to be resected.
Preoperative embolization should be performed (if surgical management is performed).
Careful hemostasis throughout procedure

Surgical management
Complete excision of osteoid osteoma with nidus leads to low recurrence rates, even if
intralesional.
En bloc marginal excision for osteoblastoma may be recommended in patients with
aggressive osteoblastomas because of the high recurrence rate.
Eosinophilic granuloma/Langerhans cell histiocytosis (Figure 7)
Benign lesion of bone
Langerhans cell histiocytosis, the preferred name, was previously called histiocytosis X. This
nomenclature includes eosinophilic granuloma. The term eosinophilic granuloma may refer
specifically to the granulomatous, inflammatory lesions of the bone.
Age: more than 80% of cases seen in individuals aged 0 to 10 years
Location: commonly vertebral body, thoracic spine

Common malignant or aggressive tumors of the spine
Chordoma (Figure 8)
Low-grade malignant tumor of spine and sacrum characterized by local invasiveness, slow
growth, and high recurrence rates; thought to originate from notochord remnants.
Can metastasize; however, metastasis often occurs late in the disease process and has not
been closely correlated with survival
Age: typically middle-aged to elderly patients
Location: commonly in clivus/sacrum, then in mobile spine
Genetic/microscopic analysis
Conventional, chondroid, or dedifferentiated
Classic histology demonstrates physaliferous cells. Overexpression of brachyury gene is a
distinguishing characteristic of chordoma.
Imaging studies
Classic imaging studies demonstrate dark appearance on T1-weighted MRIs and bright
appearance on T2-weighted MRIs, with variable but often robust enhancement with
contrast. The tumor may invade disk space and cross to neighboring vertebral bodies,
dissimilar from many other tumors of the spine.
Distinguish from benign notochordal tumors
Benign notochordal tumors (also referred to as notochordal rests or giant vertebral
notochordal rests) are benign lesions that are thought to arise from notochord
remnants but lack soft-tissue extension and typically are not destructive to bone. On
imaging studies, benign notochordal tumors may have less contrast enhancement and
appear sclerotic on CT scans. Despite some disagreement on their role as a precursor to
chordoma, surgical management typically is not indicated for these tumors.
Surgical management
En bloc excision with wide margin is the preferred treatment option.

5- and 10-year recurrence rates remain substantial, even after R0 resection.
With R0 resection in the pelvis, chordoma cells have been found as many as 2 cm away

Radiation therapy protocols vary widely.
Proton versus photon radiation therapy/stereotactic body radiation therapy
Neoadjuvant versus adjuvant radiation therapy
If resection is wide and has R0 margins, some physicians advocate irradiation of the field
to kill any remaining micrometastases in the margins. The disadvantage of this
approach is that it decreases the likelihood of bone fusion after reconstruction. Other
surgeons advocate reserving irradiation for focused therapy if recurrence is discovered
during follow-up. Neoadjuvant therapy may be effective but is associated with difficulty
of surgical incision healing.

Age: incidence peaks in individuals in their teenage years and thirties
Location: commonly thoracolumbar spine, followed by the sacrum and pelvis; rare in the
cervical spine.
Genetic/microscopic analysis: On histology, an osteoid matrix is classically found, with
other features that may classify the tumor into one of the aforementioned categories.
Numerous genetic mutations have been found in patients with osteosarcoma (eg, RB1,
TP53, c-Myc).
Imaging studies
Dark on T1-weighted MRIs, bright on T2-weighted MRIs, enhances with contrast
CT scans may reveal a combination of blastic and lytic areas.
Fluorodeoxyglucose-PET may be useful in staging because osteosarcoma typically is a
glucose-avid, PET-positive tumor.
Careful attention should be paid to chest CT scans during staging because many patients
have pulmonary metastases.
Management
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy typically is administered preoperatively.
Surgically, en bloc excision with R0 margins should be attempted if possible because it
results in improved survival and local control.
Historically, radiation therapy was reserved for palliative care only; however, advances in
radiation therapy may prove it to be a useful adjuvant treatment option.
Overall, 5-year survival after a diagnosis of spinal osteosarcoma is approximately 20% to
45%.3-5

Typically, neoadjuvant chemotherapy is administered first to shrink or control the tumor.

Recurrent or metastatic Ewing sarcoma is associated with a poor prognosis. If this occurs,

If the patient has a discrete local recurrence or solitary lesion (this can be resected

If the patient has neurologic compromise, intractable pain, or instability

Benign aggressive lesion that represents less than 5% of all primary bone tumors of the

Although termed benign, these lesions classically are locally aggressive and can metastasize
to the lungs (<5% of GCTs), which may be associated with a mortality rate as high as 20%.
Age: typically occurs in individuals aged 0 to 40 years
Location
Most commonly in the sacrum; also found throughout mobile spine, often in the vertebral
body.
Relatively equal distribution among cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine
Genetic/microscopic analysis: numerous osteoclastic giant cells in fibrous stroma; may
contain areas of hemorrhage.
Imaging studies
Classic imaging studies demonstrate an expansile, lytic lesion that may invade the disk
space, different from imaging of most other tumors.
Dark on T1-weighted MRIs, bright on T2-weighted MRIs with heterogeneous signal
because of hemorrhage/cyst degeneration
Management
Denosumab may be used as neoadjuvant therapy to shrink and solidify the tumor.
Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody to receptor activator of nuclear factor-kappa B
(RANK) ligand.
Dramatic shrinking of tumor over several weeks of denosumab management in RANK-
positive tumors6
Preoperative embolization is recommended; however, tumor vascularity often is
composed of fine vessels, and embolization may help less than expected.
Radiation therapy typically is not used because of the risk of radiation-induced sarcoma
and fairly low efficacy in terms of local control.
En bloc excision leads to much lower recurrence rates and should be performed if
possible.

Must be differentiated from telangiectatic osteosarcoma preoperatively
Because of the giant-cell-rich nature of this lesion and its RANK ligand mechanism,
denosumab (monoclonal antibody against RANK ligand) has been used by some
physicians in a manner similar to that for GCTs.
Preoperative embolization is required; however, tumor vascularity often is composed of
fine vessels, and embolization may help less than expected.
Selective embolization may serve as the sole treatment option in select patients if no
neurologic compromise or instability is present.
Radiation therapy typically is not used because of the risk of radiation-induced sarcoma
and fairly low efficacy in terms of local control.
Classically, intralesional resection has been recommended; however, recurrence rates as
high as 25% to 30% have prompted many physicians to recommend more aggressive en
bloc resection.
En bloc resection is associated with high risk but also may lead to more durable
outcomes, less recurrence, and better control of potentially life-threatening
intraoperative bleeding from the tumor. Bleeding from a tumor around the spinal cord is
difficult to control because direct pressure cannot be applied. In addition, bleeding places
the patient at risk of postoperative hematoma and potential paralysis.
The question of en bloc resection versus intralesional resection has not been resolved
and should be determined on a case-by-case basis.

Management
Multidisciplinary Approach
An experienced multidisciplinary team is critical. For example, will the patient undergo
radiation therapy preoperatively or postoperatively? Is the tumor radiosensitive or
radioresistant? Many tumors previously considered to be radioresistant currently are
managed via stereotactic body radiation therapy or proton therapy, with improved durable
control.
Typically, a spine tumor board involves expertise in neurosurgery/orthopaedic spine surgery,
radiation oncology, and interventional radiology. Although a medical oncologist typically is not
part of the spine tumor board at most institutions, communication with a medical oncologist is
critical.
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Radiosensitive disease without documented improved outcomes from surgical management in
addition to radiation therapy
Patient who cannot tolerate surgical treatment
Slowly growing tumor without neurologic compromise and/or without patient desire for
surgical treatment

Surgical Management
Indications
Primary tumor of the spine
Contraindications
Patient not a surgical candidate
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Considerations
Carefully plan approaches and steps.
Embolization of tumor
Venous duplex ultrasonography to rule out deep vein thrombosis (DVT)
If DVT is a concern, then an inferior vena cava filter should be placed preoperatively.
Placement of fiducial marker if thoracic tumor
Placement of central line preoperatively to decrease surgical time under anesthesia
Do not use cell saver; although some data suggest it is safe, recirculating potential tumor cells
is the concern.
Do not use basic metabolic panel; although it is not thought to cause malignancy, it is a potent
growth factor and typically considered best to not use in patients with a tumor.
Use tranexamic acid to decrease blood loss.
Preoperative Planning
Preoperative planning is critical. A full plan includes approaches, staging if necessary, surgical
assistance needed (eg, vascular surgeon, chest surgeon), and backup plans.
The author of this lesson typically lists all the steps of the day on the wall along with a list of
special materials that may be needed during the procedure.
Weinstein-Boriani-Biagini staging also is used to help guide resection.
Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry is useful to understand bone quality preoperatively.
Cement augmentation via fenestrated screws is useful in patients with poor bone quality.

Bed, head holder

Intraoperative monitoring is important for long procedures, especially those involving
somatosensory evoked potentials, which can detect potential positioning problems during
long procedures.
Surgical Approaches
Overall surgical pearls
Use meticulous hemostasis throughout the procedure.
Use multiple hemostatic agents to prepare for blood loss from tumor.
Soak the field in sterile water after resection of the tumor to lyse any potential free-floating
tumor cells.
Be prepared for quick control of tumor spillage if it occurs.
En bloc resection
Anterior, lateral, and posterior approaches are used, often in staged fashion.
En bloc spondylectomy is a morbid procedure with a high risk profile, even for the most
experienced surgeons. Patients should be counseled extensively on the risks of the
procedure and should be prepared mentally for a complication or revision surgery.
Soft-tissue closure from flap or closure by a plastic surgery team may be warranted.
Surgical procedures involving skin that has been or will be irradiated often leads to
difficulty with wound healing. In most patients, the author of this lesson prefers adjuvant
radiation therapy (postoperative) if indicated, only after the incision has healed (usually
approximately 4 weeks postoperatively).
Removing a segment of mobile spine in this manner may be tricky, and care should be
taken to protect the spinal cord at all times.
Bleeding from around the spinal cord may be problematic and, in patients with tumor
bleeding, life-threatening.
Because of removal of the entire segment of the spine at a level and in anticipation of
adjuvant therapies (radiation therapy, chemotherapy), robust constructs should be used.
Circumferential reconstruction is almost always preferred.
Fusion may be difficult to achieve, and the use of vascularized strut grafts may promote
long-term fusion.

Postoperative Management
Postoperative intensive care for neurologic assessment and overall management
Given the length of the procedure, patients may remain intubated overnight postoperatively.
Chemoprophylaxis for DVT/pulmonary embolism will be necessary postoperatively in these
patients, and most surgeons favor waiting 24 to 48 hours before initiating chemoprophylaxis
to reduce the risk of postoperative hematoma.
Drains should be assessed for extensive output and for changes in color or consistency.
White color: concern for chylothorax
Purulent output: concern for infection
Pitfalls and Preventive Measures
Patient counseling
Given the high risk, patients and their families should be adequately prepared for a
complication postoperatively.
Complications
DVT/venous thromboembolism: minimize surgical time if possible, chemoprophylaxis in
addition to mechanical prophylaxis
Neurologic injury or weakness: careful work around neural elements, realistic patient
expectations if sacrificing root or if potential for weakness exists
Other complications: extensive patient counseling given complications with these surgical
procedures
Tumor spillage: rapid patch over site of tumor spill, soak in sterile water
Nonunion/hardware failure: robust circumferential reconstruction
Wound dehiscence/infection: careful soft-tissue handling/flap or plastic surgery closure
Hematoma: meticulous hemostasis intraoperatively, postoperative drains
